newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- DEC 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- DEC 18.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:
KATHIMERINI

--Falling tourist exchange inflows and decreased European Union funds have led to a sudden increase in the balance of the current accounts deficit. According to unofficial estimates, the deficit will be over four billion dollars at the end of 1996, against 2.9 billion at the end of 1995. The Bank of Greece is expected to announce the figures tomorrow.
--Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas's appeal to EU farm commissioner Franz Fischler for compensation for farmers whose crops were lost or damaged in freak storms recently has been turned down.

--The central bank held back from intervening in the reduction of interest rates in the interbank market. The National Mortgage Bank on the other hand cut its interest rates on housing loans by o.50 percent on fixed rates and 0.25 percent on variable rates.

--Deputy Development Minister Mihalis Chrysohoidis's decision to bolster the insurance companies' auxiliary fund with assets of insurance companies that have closed will mean an inflow of four billion drachmas, sources say.
IMERISIA

--The balance of payments will close this year at a record 4.3 billion dollars (3.1 percent of GDP), an increase of 48 percent over the previous year, sources say. The major worry over the fall in revenues concerns less tourist exchange, attributed mainly to the hard drachma policy.

--The Bank of Greece's move yesterday to reduce its discount and overdraft rates while leaving the lombard and overnight rates untouched sends a message to financial markets of its intent to put a brake on credit expansion.

--The decision to see the Bank of Attica has been clinched, indicating the start of the sell-off of smaller banks announced by the government. An official announcement is expected today by National Economy and Finance Minister Yiannos Papantoniou.
KERDOS

--Inflation may fall further in December, despite the ongoing farmers' blockades. Sources say Athens is in no danger of running out of supplies as farmers are letting through fresh food and meat on the side. National economy ministry sources, meanwhile, are confident that inflation could fall below 7.5 percent.
--The judicial investigation into the Delta Securities scandal reaches its final stages.
EXPRESS

--Tomorrow will be the crucial day in the farmers' blockade as they and their families descend on Athens. Government and business hope that the march and rally tomorrow will be the pinacle of the protests, with no way to go but down from there. Farmers, however, are counting on a second wind with their protest.
--Seamen and dockworkers declared a new additional 48-hour strike yesterday, following a fruitless meeting with Merchant Marine Minister Stavros Soumakis yesterday.
--Twelve financial derivates will come under the taxation department's scrutiny soon for the imposition of taxes.
NAFTEMBORIKI

--Papandoniou told Reuters yesterday he was confident that the government would achieve budget targets for inflation this month and next year. Papandoniou is expected to reiterate these comments in the budget debate in Parliament today.

--The central bank is attempting the freeze the cost of money, sending a message to the govvernment to proceed cautiously with the de-escalation of interest rates with its decision yesterday to not reduce the interbank overnight rate. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
